content.title: Substring with Concatenation of All Words

blocks.text: Given a string s and an array of strings words, all of the same length, return all the starting indices of substrings in s that are a concatenation of every word in words exactly once, in any order, with no extra characters in between.

blocks.caption: Slide a word-level window; find every starting index where every word is used exactly once

blocks.text: Given a string s and a list of equal-length words, find every starting index in s where the characters starting there form an exact back-to-back concatenation of all the words, each used exactly once, in any order.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Word-Search Puzzle With Fixed-Length Tiles
blocks.text: Like laying down a strip of fixed-length letter tiles (the words, in any order, used exactly once each) directly against a long ribbon of text, and finding every position along the ribbon where the tiles line up perfectly with no gaps or overlaps and no leftover tiles unused.

blocks.caption: Different starting offsets can never share word boundaries, so each offset needs its own independent window

blocks.text: Before checking every possible substring position from scratch, notice that every word has the same fixed length, which means whole words, not individual characters, can be treated as the unit the window works over.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Since every word has the same length, any valid match is a sequence of exactly len(words) word-sized chunks placed back to back, with no gaps.

Observation 2: This becomes exactly the "at most/exactly k of each kind" frequency-matching technique from Permutation in String, just applied to whole words instead of individual characters.

Observation 3: A valid match's starting index must fall on one of wordLen possible "phases" (offset 0, 1, ..., wordLen-1), since word boundaries can never straddle across different phases. Each phase needs its own completely independent word-level sliding window.

Observation 4: Within a single phase, slide a window word-chunk by word-chunk, tracking a frequency map of words currently inside it; when a chunk isn't a needed word at all, the window must reset entirely, since no match can span across it; when a word's count exceeds what's needed, shrink from the left (word-chunk by word-chunk) until it's back in bounds; when exactly len(words) words are held, record the window's start as a match.

Recognizing the fixed word length as a reason to operate one level up, on whole words rather than characters, is what turns an apparently expensive multi-string matching problem into a linear, word-level sliding window.
This is Permutation in String's exact-frequency-matching sliding window technique, generalized to whole words and run independently across every possible word-alignment phase.
For every possible starting index, slice out each word-sized chunk directly and check whether the multiset of chunks exactly matches the required words.

items: For every possible starting index (where a full concatenation could still fit), slice out numWords consecutive word-sized chunks.
Track a frequency map of chunks seen so far at this starting index; abandon immediately if a chunk isn't needed at all, or if any chunk's count exceeds what's required.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: A fresh frequency map is built for every starting index, since each independent check needs its own word-count tracking.
The inner loop breaks immediately once a chunk is found that isn't needed, or that exceeds its required count, since neither can ever be fixed by continuing.
Only starting indices where a full concatenation could even fit (start + totalLen <= n) are checked at all.

blocks.text: Every possible starting index is checked directly by slicing and validating its word chunks, so every correct match is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n * numWords * wordLen) in the worst case, since each of roughly n starting indices slices and checks up to numWords chunks, each of length wordLen.
Space: O(numWords) for the frequency maps.

Limitation: resumming the frequency map from scratch for every starting index ignores that shifting the starting index by one word-length only changes a single leaving and a single entering word chunk, which can be tracked incrementally instead.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force rebuilds its word-frequency map from scratch at every starting index. Instead, run one sliding window per possible alignment phase (offset 0 through wordLen - 1). Within each phase, slide the window forward one whole word-chunk at a time, maintaining a running frequency map: add the entering chunk, and if a chunk that isn't needed at all appears, reset the window entirely (since no match can span across a completely foreign chunk); if a needed chunk's count exceeds its requirement, shrink from the left one word-chunk at a time; whenever the window holds exactly numWords words, record its start as a match and shrink by one word-chunk to keep sliding.

For each of the wordLen possible phases, maintain a window over word-chunks (not characters) with a running frequency map. Grow by adding the entering chunk. Reset the window entirely on an unneeded chunk. Shrink from the left, one word-chunk at a time, whenever a chunk's count exceeds its requirement. Record a match whenever the window holds exactly numWords words, then shrink by one to continue sliding.
Run a word-level sliding window independently for each possible alignment phase, tracking a running frequency map of word-chunks.
Dry run for s = "barfoothefoobarman", words = ["foo","bar"] (wordLen=3, numWords=2), phase offset=0

blocks.title: Other phases
blocks.text: Phase offset=1 and offset=2 produce no matches at all here, since every 3-character chunk starting at those offsets (e.g. "arf", "oot", "hef", ...) is not one of the needed words. Combining all phases gives the final result [0, 9].

codes.python:
def find_substring(s, words):
    word_len = len(words[0])
    num_words = len(words)
    n = len(s)
    need = {}
    for w in words:
        need[w] = need.get(w, 0) + 1
    result = []
    for offset in range(word_len):                                          # try every possible word-boundary alignment
        left = offset
        count = 0
        window = {}
        right = offset
        while right + word_len <= n:
            piece = s[right:right + word_len]
            if piece in need:
                window[piece] = window.get(piece, 0) + 1
                count += 1
                while window[piece] > need[piece]:                          # too many of this word, shrink from the left
                    left_piece = s[left:left + word_len]
                    window[left_piece] -= 1
                    left += word_len
                    count -= 1
                if count == num_words:                                      # every word matched exactly, record this start
                    result.append(left)
                    left_piece = s[left:left + word_len]
                    window[left_piece] -= 1
                    left += word_len
                    count -= 1
            else:
                window.clear()                                              # a totally foreign word breaks any alignment through it
                count = 0
                left = right + word_len
            right += word_len
    return result


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(find_substring("barfoothefoobarman", ["foo", "bar"]))

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n * wordLen) total across all phases combined, since each phase scans roughly n/wordLen chunks in O(wordLen) each (for the substring slice), and there are wordLen phases.
Space: O(numWords) for the frequency maps.

Since every word has the same fixed length, any valid concatenation match must align its word boundaries with one of exactly wordLen possible "phases" relative to the start of s; running an independent word-level sliding window per phase, using the same exact-frequency-matching technique as Permutation in String but one level up (on whole words instead of characters), guarantees every valid match is found exactly once, in whichever phase it aligns with.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["Chunk is not one of the needed words at all","No match can span across it; reset the window completely and continue from just after it"],["Chunk is needed, but its count would exceed the requirement","Shrink from the left, one word-chunk at a time, until it's back in bounds"],["Window holds exactly numWords words, matching every requirement exactly","Record the window's start as a match, then shrink by one chunk to keep sliding"]]}

items: The outer loop over offset ensures every possible word-boundary alignment is checked, since a match can never span across chunks from two different phases.
window.clear() on an unneeded chunk is essential, since a completely foreign word chunk invalidates every match candidate that would span across it, not just the ones ending exactly there.
Recording a match and then shrinking by exactly one word-chunk (rather than resetting entirely) allows overlapping matches within the same phase to still be found.

blocks.text: Recognizing that a fixed word length lets whole words be treated as the sliding window's unit, and that valid matches can only align to one of wordLen phases, generalizes the exact-frequency-matching technique from Permutation in String up to the word level.

items: Forgetting to run a separate window for every possible phase (offset), which misses valid matches that don't align to a multiple of wordLen from the very start of s.
Shrinking the window by only part of a word-chunk instead of a full chunk at a time, which breaks the word-alignment invariant.
Not fully resetting the window (map, count, and left pointer) upon encountering a completely unneeded chunk, which can let stale counts leak into a match that shouldn't be valid.

items: Explicitly connect this problem to Permutation in String before coding, framing it as "the same exact-frequency-matching window, but one level up on whole words, across every possible alignment phase", since this framing demonstrates pattern-recognition rather than treating it as an unrelated hard problem.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Find substrings that are an exact concatenation of a list of equal-length words, in any order" points toward a word-level sliding window with exact frequency matching, run independently across every possible word-alignment phase.

items: What if the words could have different lengths? The whole word-level windowing technique breaks down, since there's no longer a fixed chunk size to slide by; a substantially different approach (e.g., trie-based matching) would be needed.

How would you optimize further if words contains many duplicates? Deduplicating words into a frequency map upfront (already done here via `need`) avoids redundant work regardless of how many duplicates exist.

What's the point of running wordLen separate phases instead of one single character-level window? A single character-level window can't guarantee word-chunk alignment; two windows a single phase apart could otherwise "false match" by combining fragments of two different words.
A direct generalization of Permutation in String's exact-frequency-matching sliding window, applied to whole words instead of characters, and run across every possible alignment phase.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n * numWords * wordLen) time, O(numWords) space.
Optimized (word-level sliding window per phase): O(n * wordLen) time, O(numWords) space.

items: Pattern: Word-level variable/fixed-size sliding window with exact frequency matching, run across every possible word-alignment phase
Core Idea: Treat each word-sized chunk as a unit; slide word-chunk by word-chunk, matching the required word multiset exactly, once per alignment phase
Time: O(n * wordLen)
Space: O(numWords)
Most Important Observation: A fixed word length means valid matches can only align to one of wordLen phases, and each phase needs its own independent word-level window
Interview Difficulty: Hard
